rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: ʿAlī reports that the Prophet taught each person's destination is recorded, then urged action because everyone is eased toward what they were created for; he recited these verses.

rows.speaker: al-Zamakhsharī
rows.claim: Al-Zamakhsharī explains that God makes the way to obedience amiable and grants success until obedience becomes easiest, like God's expanding a guided person's breast for submission.
rows.anchor: al-Zamakhsharī says that the meaning is, “We will make it amiable to him and grant him success until obedience [to God] becomes the easiest

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most understand giving as charitable giving; it can also mean giving God His proper due.
rows.anchor: Gives is understood by most to mean giving in charity, but can also indicate giving God His proper due (Sh).

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most take al-ḥusnā as the testimony that there is no god but God; another gloss is belief in God, either of which is attested to or denied.
rows.anchor: is taken by most to mean “There is no god but God” (Sh) or simply belief in God (Z)

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others understand al-ḥusnā as Paradise, called the most beautiful reward in 3:148 and 3:195.
rows.anchor: others see it as a reference to Paradise, which is referred to as the most beautiful reward in 3:148 and 3:195

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥusnā can also refer to God Himself, whose Most Beautiful Names are affirmed in several verses.
rows.anchor: it can also be seen as a reference to God Himself, for, as several verses attest, Unto Him belong the Most Beautiful Names

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ease is linked to God's desire for ease rather than hardship and to reverence, through which God appoints ease in one's affairs.
rows.anchor: ease in one’s affairs derives from reverence, as in 65:4: And whosoever reverences God, He will appoint ease for his affair.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although “self-sufficient” is literal, “deems himself beyond need” conveys the negative illusion of independence from God.
rows.anchor: but beyond need better conveys the negative connotation of viewing oneself

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Miserliness toward those below and imagined independence from what is above invert the proper balance: obedience to God and generosity toward others.
rows.anchor: Being miserly toward those below one’s station and having the illusion of self-sufficiency in relation to what is above is an inversion of the proper balance

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥusnā can mean the Garden's reward, the Garden's reality, God's Reality, or all three; the discussion also applies to 92:6.
rows.anchor: What is most beautiful here can mean the reward of the Garden, the reality of the Garden itself, the Reality of God, or all three

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Turning away in disobedience brings reciprocity just as turning to God in repentance does; many gloss hardship as evil.
rows.anchor: Just as there is reciprocity when turning to God in repentance, so too there is reciprocity when turning away from God in disobedience. Hardship is glossed by many with “evil”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelief and evil deeds can open the way to further evil until returning becomes harder, as the different natures of good and evil deeds in verse 4 imply.
rows.anchor: when people disbelieve and commit evil deeds, God opens the way for them to commit further evil and it becomes increasingly difficult to turn back

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The clause may instead be rendered as a rhetorical question asking what wealth will avail when its owner perishes.
rows.anchor: Alternately, “What will his wealth avail him when he perishes?”

rows.speaker: IK and Ṭ
rows.claim: “Perishes” may refer either to dying or to entering the Fire.
rows.anchor: Perishes can be taken to mean when he dies or when he enters the Fire (IK, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: several commentators
rows.claim: Commentators tell of a Medinan palm owner who snatched fallen dates from a poor family's children and refused the Prophet's offer of a Paradise palm; another man paid forty palms, donated the tree, and the Prophet gave it to the family. The refusal maps to vv. 15–16, the gift to vv. 18–21.
rows.anchor: Several commentators say that the whole of this sūrah was revealed in reference to a Muslim of Madinah who had a palm tree

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: If this is an early Makkan sūrah, the palm-tree story likely is not its occasion; the verses instead generally condemn those who rejected Muhammad as prophet.
rows.anchor: If, however, this is an early Makkan sūrah, as some maintain

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving charity in God's name purifies both the giver and the wealth; tazakkā shares an etymological root with zakāh.
rows.anchor: one purifies both oneself and one’s wealth when one gives charity in the Name of God. To purify translates tazakkā, which is etymologically related to the Quranic word for alms, zakāh

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say vv. 17–21 praise Abū Bakr, who bought and freed weak slaves; when his father asked why he did not buy stronger defenders, he said he sought no defense.
rows.anchor: others say that vv. 18–21 were revealed about the first Caliph, Abū Bakr al-Ṣiddīq, who used to buy weak slaves and then free them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One revelation account says Bilāl was tortured after desecrating the Kaʿbah idols, kept testifying to God's oneness, and the Prophet assured him that the One would save him.
rows.anchor: One account of the revelation of these verses states that, upon embracing Islam, Bilāl, who was a slave of one ʿAbd Allāh ibn Judan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In that account Abū Bakr bought Bilāl for gold after the Prophet told him Bilāl was tortured for God; the idolaters alleged he acted to repay a favor, prompting vv. 19–21.
rows.anchor: The Prophet came upon this and said to him, “The One will save you!” He then informed Abū Bakr, saying,“Bilāl is being tortured for the sake of God!

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Bilāl later became the first to lead the call to prayer and one of the Prophet's personal treasurers.
rows.anchor: Bilāl later became the first to lead the call to prayer

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse literally says no one has a favor with him to repay: he neither repays past favors nor expects future recompense, but gives only to seek God's will.
rows.anchor: This verse literally reads, “no one having with him any favor to be repaid.” In both translations the implication is that one is neither recompensing others for favors

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Ḍuḥā is early Makkan and ranked fourth by many, seventh by others; it may be the first sūrah revealed whole, though others give that distinction to al-Fātiḥah.
rows.anchor: considered by many commentators to be fourth (others say seventh) in the chronological order of revelation and perhaps the first sūrah to be revealed in full at one time

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: The title most commonly means the rising sun's light; it can also mean the period from daybreak to noon, the whole sunlit day, or all creation made visible by sunlight. It also names a late-morning supererogatory prayer.
rows.anchor: most common understanding of al-ḍuḥā as a reference to the light of the rising sun, but it can also refer to the period from daybreak until noon

rows.speaker: several commentators
rows.claim: One occasion account says revelation paused for twelve, forty, or fifty days, after which an idolater taunted Muhammad that his satan had forsaken him, prompting reassurance.
rows.anchor: According to several commentators, the Prophet had not received a revelation for some time (some say twelve days, others forty, and others fifty)

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another account says idolaters declared that Muhammad's Lord had forsaken and despised him.
rows.anchor: Others say that it was in response to several idolaters saying, “Surely Muhammad’s lord has forsaken him and despised him”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further account says illness kept the Prophet from night vigil for two or three nights; Umm Jamīl, Abū Lahab's wife, taunted him, and vv. 1–3 were revealed.
rows.anchor: the Prophet became sick and could not offer his supererogatory night vigil

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah consoles the Prophet: it assures him God will not abandon him, recalls God's favors, and ends by urging care for the downtrodden and preaching the message.
rows.anchor: The main theme of the sūrah is consolation of the Prophet. It begins with an assertion that God would not abandon the Prophet

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Some identify morning brightness with the morning God spoke to Moses and night with the Night Journey and Ascension; others identify it as the moment Moses' opponents recognized truth and prostrated.
rows.anchor: others say al-ḍuḥā refers to the hour at which

rows.speaker: al-Shawkānī
rows.claim: When al-ḍuḥā precedes the night, al-Shawkānī says it refers to the whole day.
rows.anchor: According to al-Shawkānī, when al-ḍuḥā precedes the mention of night, as in this context, it refers to the entire day.

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Other symbolic readings make morning the Garden's light and night the Fire's darkness, or light in knowers' hearts and blackness in disbelievers' hearts.
rows.anchor: It is also said that al-ḍuḥā is the light of the Garden and the night is the darkness of the Fire

rows.speaker: Sh and Ṭ
rows.claim: “When still” may describe darkness spreading across the day; night may also mean as it approaches or as it leaves.
rows.anchor: When still is said to refer to the darkness as it extends over the day

rows.speaker: Sh and Ṭ
rows.claim: The night is also interpreted as the night approaching or departing.
rows.anchor: V. 2 is also interpreted to mean, “The night as it approaches” or “The night as it leaves” (Sh, Ṭ).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse is the response to the oath.
rows.anchor: This verse constitutes what is known as the response to the oath.

rows.speaker: most
rows.claim: Most supply “thee” as the implied object of “despise,” though the Arabic omits it; the clause can instead generalize that despising is not in God's nature.
rows.anchor: Although most interpret the second-person singular (thee) to be the implied direct object of despise, it is not present in the Arabic text.

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most call al-Sharḥ Makkan and place it just after Sūrah 93; Ibn ʿAbbās calls it Madinan, while some assign only vv. 5–6 to Madinah.
rows.anchor: considered by most commentators to be a Makkan sūrah, most likely revealed immediately after the preceding one. Ibn ʿAbbās is reported to have said that it is Madinan

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from the expansion of the breast for religion in its first verse.
rows.anchor: It takes its name from the reference to the expansion of the breast for religion in the first verse.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Some say Sūrahs 93 and 94 were originally one, since Companions recited them together in one prayer cycle without a basmalah separating them.
rows.anchor: the Companions of the Prophet would recite them together in a single prayer cycle

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Linguistically, 94:1 follows the same pattern as 93:6, with the construction also implied in 93:7–8.
rows.anchor: Linguistically 94:1 follows the same pattern as 93:6, Did He not find thee . . ., which is also implied in 93:7–8.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Both sūrahs present God's bounties as relief: Sūrah 93 addresses external needs, Sūrah 94 spiritual relief; 94 recalls blessings, reassures, then commands exertion and turning to God.
rows.anchor: Thematically both sūrahs speak of the bounties that God has provided the Prophet Muhammad as relief for the difficulties that beset him

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verses can mean that patiently enduring hardship brings ease in both this life and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: These verses can be read as indicating that enduring hardship with patience results in ease in this life and the Hereafter.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A well-known hadith says one instance of hardship never overcomes two instances of ease.
rows.anchor: One instance of hardship (ʿusr

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The claim is linked to God's promise to bring ease after hardship and desire ease rather than hardship for people.
rows.anchor: Also see, 65:7: God tasks no soul beyond that which He has given it. God will bring ease after hardship; and 2:185: God desires ease for you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Tīn is likely an early-middle Makkan sūrah revealed after Sūrah 85, though some consider it Madinan; it is named for the fig in verse 1.
rows.anchor: A Makkan sūrah, al-Tīn was most likely revealed in the early part of the middle Makkan period, shortly after Sūrah 85

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 4–6 describe humanity's exalted origin and fall when people fail to live by their true nature, a message like 103:2–3.
rows.anchor: The main theme is found in vv. 4–6, which are among the most famous verses in the Quran. They speak to the human condition

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says whoever recites the sūrah through its closing question and answers “Indeed” is among its witnesses.
rows.anchor: According to an oft citedḥadīth, the Prophet said, “Whosoever among you recites By the fig and the olive through to is not God the most just of judges

rows.speaker: most commentators
rows.claim: Most commentators take the fig and olive as earthly fruits, sworn by for their blessings and benefits.
rows.anchor: For most commentators, the fig and the olive refer to the fruits of the earth, by which God swears due to the blessing and benefits contained in them

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Some read them symbolically: fig as Damascus's mosque, perhaps Noah's mosque at Mount Jūdī, and olive as Jerusalem's Holy House; others identify the two mountains or cities.
rows.anchor: the fig symbolizes the mosque (meaning place of prostration, as there would not have been a building for that purpose at the time of the revelation) in Damascus

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Another interpretation makes the fig the mosque of the Companions of the Cave and the olive the mosque in Jerusalem; another sees two Levantine mountains.
rows.anchor: Another interpretation takes the fig as a reference to the “mosque” of the Companions of the Cave (18:9) and the olive as a reference to the “mosque” in Jerusalem

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: A further view makes the fig the Garden leaves Adam and Eve used to cover themselves and the olive the blessed tree; these may foreshadow human abasement and intellect's light.
rows.anchor: Others say that the fig refers to the leaves of the Garden (7:22), with which Adam and Eve covered themselves, and the olive refers to the blessed olive tree in 24:35

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse answers the oath in vv. 1–3 and affirms humanity's exalted status, reflected in the angels' command to prostrate to Adam.
rows.anchor: This verse begins the response to the oath taken in vv. 1–3. It is one of the most emphatic affirmations of humanity’s exalted status

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although made of clay, the human being is proportioned and receives God's Spirit.
rows.anchor: Although the human being is made of clay, God declares in 38:72, I have proportioned him and breathed into him of My Spirit.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Man” means all humanity, female and male, believers and disbelievers.
rows.anchor: Here man is taken to mean all of humanity, male and female, believer and disbeliever alike.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Taqwīm, from qawwama, means raising, shaping, forming, or arranging; here it describes achieving harmonious balance and becoming what one ought to be.
rows.anchor: Taqwīm, translated stature, is a verbal noun from the verb qawwama, “to raise, shape, form, or arrange.” Here it is taken to indicate something that has become what it truly ought to be

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One sign of this stature is that humans stand upright while other creatures have faces bent down.
rows.anchor: An indication of this stature is that the human being stands upright while every other creature is created with his face stooped down

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Beautiful stature is more than bodily form: the physical symbolizes inner comportment, and humans are God's best creation outwardly and inwardly.
rows.anchor: the physical is also a symbol of

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith qudsī that God created Adam in His image is understood to mean humans reflect Divine Attributes such as life, knowledge, power, will, speech, hearing, and sight.
rows.anchor: as expressed in a famous ḥadīth qudsī, “Truly God created Adam in His image”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Humans can manifest all Divine Names and Qualities, unlike other creatures; philosophers call humanity a microcosm containing all created entities.
rows.anchor: “For this reason the philosophers say that [man] is a microcosm, since all that makes up created entities is gathered within him”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 30:8 and 51:21 call people to reflect on and live according to their exalted status; if vv. 1–3 refer to revelation's locations, stature means receptivity to revelation.
rows.anchor: Verses such as 30:8 and 51:21 can be seen as a call to human beings to reflect upon their exalted status and live in accord with it.

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Outwardly, the verse can mean old age, when faculties diminish, sometimes into decrepitude, as in the parallel about long life causing regression.
rows.anchor: With regard to the outward human form, this verse can be seen as a reference to old age, when faculties are diminished, sometimes to the point of decrepitude

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Inwardly, it can mean people fall below their true nature and are cast into the Fire for failing the demands of their beautiful creation.
rows.anchor: With regard to the inner reality, it can be taken as a reference to human beings falling below their true nature and consequently being cast into the Fire

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: The phrase can describe disbelievers, who are lower than cattle, or the place into which they are cast.
rows.anchor: the lowest of the low can be understood as a reference to the state of disbelievers, of whom 7:179 says, Such as these are like cattle

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some read the phrase as “the lowest, lowly,” with lowly describing abasement and implying that the condemned condition itself brought them down.
rows.anchor: According to some, the lowest of the low should be read

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The exception for believers makes it more likely that the preceding verse describes an inner spiritual fall.
rows.anchor: This verse makes it more likely that the preceding verse refers to the inner reality of human beings.

rows.speaker: R
rows.claim: An unceasing reward is never diminished or cut off in this life or the next.
rows.anchor: A reward unceasing (cf. 41:8; 68:3; 84:25) is one that is never decreased or cut off in this life or the next

rows.speaker: Āl and Q
rows.claim: In this life, continued religious practice earns worship's reward even when illness prevents performance or travel requires shortened prayers or breaking the fast, as Islamic law permits.
rows.anchor: if people maintain religious practice, they continue to receive reward for required acts of worship even when sickness renders them unable to perform them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: For the next life, the unceasing reward refers to Heaven's bounties.
rows.anchor: Regarding the next world, it refers to the bounties of Heaven.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qāriʿah is Makkan and likely followed Sūrah 106; some regard “the Calamity” as a name for Judgment Day.
rows.anchor: Makkan sūrah, most likely revealed just after Sūrah 106

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: The calamity is considered by some to be one of the names of the Day of Judgment; vv. 1–5 vividly describe the earth's destruction then.
rows.anchor: which according to some is one of the names of the Day of Judgment. The first five verses provide a vivid description of the destruction of the earth

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The final six verses contrast the recompense of those whose scales are heavy with good deeds and those whose scales are light.
rows.anchor: The last six verses (vv. 6–11) contrast the recompense

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The scales are heavy with good deeds.
rows.anchor: Scales are heavy with good deeds.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Mawāzīn is plural of mīzān: the Qur'an uses balance for revelation and revealed just order, but scales for weighing deeds at Resurrection.
rows.anchor: is employed in the Quran to indicate revelation itself

rows.speaker: Āl
rows.claim: Although the plural suggests each person's experience of weighing, most say one scale weighs all deeds.
rows.anchor: The plural, scales, speaks to how each individual will experience the weighing of his or her deeds, but according to most, it is in fact one scale

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Good and evil deeds are unequal; good deeds remove evil deeds, and a good deed earns tenfold while an evil deed is repaid only in kind.
rows.anchor: From a Quranic perspective, the good deed and the evil deed are not equal (41:34), and good deeds remove those that are evil (11:114).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A hadith says nothing placed in the Balance weighs more heavily than good character.
rows.anchor: There is nothing placed in the Balance that is heavier than goodness of character

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says deeds are judged according to intentions, and each person receives what was intended.
rows.anchor: another ḥadīth states, “Deeds are only in accord with their intentions. And every person has only what he intended.”

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A hadith says no one enters Paradise through deeds alone; when asked whether this included him, the Prophet said only God's mercy would shelter him.
rows.anchor: As a ḥadīth states, “None of you will enter Paradise by his deeds.” Someone asked, “Not even you, O Messenger of God?”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contenting life of the person with heavy scales is linked to 69:21.
rows.anchor: For he shall enjoy a life contenting, cf. 69:21.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The light scales and abyss are linked to 7:9 and 23:103.
rows.anchor: For one whose scales are light, cf. 7:9; 23:103.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “Mother” translates umm, from amma, to betake oneself or direct one's course; here evildoers direct themselves to Hell's abyss.
rows.anchor: Mother translates umm, which derives from the verb amma, meaning, “to betake oneself to” or “direct one’s course to.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This resembles verses about people wronging themselves and verses describing Hell or Fire as disbelievers' refuge.
rows.anchor: In this sense it is similar to verses that speak of those who wrong themselves

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most consider al-Takāthur Makkan and place it after al-Kawthar; a minority call it Madinan.
rows.anchor: al-Takāthur is a Makkan sūrah, believed to follow Sūrah 108

rows.speaker: some Companions
rows.claim: Some Companions reportedly called this “The Sūrah of the Grave.”
rows.anchor: was reportedly called “The Sūrah of the Grave” by some Companions of the Prophet

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The best-attested occasion concerns Banū ʿAbd Manāf and Banū Sahm boasting about numbers, counting the living then dead; Sahm prevailed because it had more pre-Islamic dead.
rows.anchor: this sūrah was revealed about two clans of the Quraysh

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Others say the verses address the People of the Book, specifically the Jews of Madinah.
rows.anchor: Others say that these verses are a reference to the People of the Book or specifically to the Jews of Madinah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The first two verses expose delusion in accumulating worldly goods, a theme elsewhere in the Qur'an; vv. 3–8 warn persistent accumulators they will know Hellfire with certainty.
rows.anchor: The first two verses speak of the delusion of accumulating worldly goods, which is referenced throughout the Quran

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Competing for worldly gains distracts people from obeying God and remembering the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: Vying for increase in worldly gains distracts people from obedience to God and remembering the Hereafter

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Lahw, “distraction,” is amusement that keeps people from reaching their real goals.
rows.anchor: indicates an amusement, something that keeps people from achieving their real goals

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur'an warns against worldly life deluding people.
rows.anchor: In this vein, the Quran advises, Let not the life of this world delude you

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Takāthur means competing and boasting over anything sought for ego gratification rather than God's sake.
rows.anchor: Vying for increase translates takāthur, which implies both competing and boasting. It can pertain to anything that people seek for the gratification of their egos

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: A saying attributed to the Prophet defines takāthur as unjustly gathering wealth, withholding what is due, and hoarding it.
rows.anchor: According to a saying attributed to the Prophet, it means gathering wealth without right, withholding it from those to whom it rightfully belongs, and hoarding it

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: When a Companion found the Prophet reciting the verse, he said wealth benefits a person only as food eaten, clothes worn, or charity spent.
rows.anchor: the Prophet said, “The son of Adam says, ‘My wealth! My wealth!’ But do you get anything from your wealth except what you have eaten and finished

rows.speaker: the Prophet
rows.claim: Another hadith says that if Adam's son had a valley of gold, he would want a second valley.
rows.anchor: Another ḥadīth states, “If the son of Adam had a valley of gold, he would wish for it to be two valleys”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse may refer to the clans' graveyard boasting, or to distraction continuing without repentance until people die.
rows.anchor: This verse can be interpreted according to the first occasion of revelation mentioned in the sūrah introduction or as implying that people will continue to be distracted and not repent before they die

rows.speaker: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib
rows.claim: ʿAlī condemns graveyard visitors for drawing pride from ancestors' dead bodies and numbers instead of taking lessons that should inspire humility.
rows.anchor: ʿAlī ibn Abī Ṭālib is reported to have said, “How neglectful are these visitors and how difficult is the affair.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ʿAṣr is Makkan and likely follows Sūrah 94; ʿaṣr can mean late afternoon, its last hour, afternoon, the afternoon prayer, or an epoch.
rows.anchor: most likely follows Sūrah 94

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Companions reportedly did not part after meeting until one recited the whole sūrah and greeted the other with peace.
rows.anchor: whenever two Companions of the Prophet would meet they would not part company until one of them had recited al-ʿAṣr in its entirety

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Read after Sūrah 102, ʿaṣr can mean time generally: vying for increase wastes it, and time's blessing is what people will be questioned about.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These three short verses can be seen as the whole Qur'an's message: humanity loses unless it turns to God.
rows.anchor: From one perspective, these three short verses contain the entire message of the Quran, namely, that human beings are in loss unless they turn to God.

rows.speaker: al-Shāfiʿī
rows.claim: Al-Shāfiʿī is reported to have said that if people pondered this sūrah, it would suffice them.
rows.anchor: the famous legal scholar al-Shāfiʿī is reported to have said,“Were the people to ponder this sūrah, it would suffice them”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: ʿAṣr derives from ʿaṣara, “to squeeze,” and evokes time declining or fading quickly.
rows.anchor: Linguistically, ʿaṣr derives from the verb ʿaṣara, meaning “to squeeze,” and thus relates to time that is declining or fading quickly.

rows.speaker: many
rows.claim: Many take it as the ʿaṣr prayer, identified with the “middlemost prayer” in 2:238, though that verse has other interpretations.
rows.anchor: many judge the most likely to be the ʿaṣr prayer (Bḍ, Q, Z), which is considered to be the prayer referred to as the middlemost prayer in 2:238

rows.speaker: some
rows.claim: Some understand ʿaṣr as the Prophet's era, blessed by the renewal of prophethood.
rows.anchor: Some also say the term in this verse refers to the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This reading applies to individuals and humanity's history: each generation falls a degree below the previous one.
rows.anchor: the fall of humanity continues as the historical cycle unfolds, and each generation is a degree below the generation before it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 2–3 answer the oath and parallel 95:5–6.
rows.anchor: Vv. 2–3 are the response to the oath in v. 1 and are similar in meaning to 95:5–6

rows.speaker: Bg and Q
rows.claim: Mankind can mean disbelievers; another reading takes it as humanity generally.
rows.anchor: The term mankind can be seen as a reference to disbelievers (Bg, Q) or to humanity in general (Q).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In light of the declining day, mankind can refer to humanity in the final phase of the historical cycle.
rows.anchor: Seen in light of the reference to the declining day, it can also be taken as a reference to humanity during the latter days of the historical cycle.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelief increases disbelievers only in loss; Qur'anic loss encompasses both this world and the Hereafter.
rows.anchor: the disbelief of the disbelievers increases them in naught but loss

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Losers lose what they value most in this life, not necessarily material goods, and later lose their souls and families at Resurrection.
rows.anchor: The losers are thus those who lose what they value most in this life, although not necessarily purely material things, and in the next life

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Spiritually, loss can mean losing faith and attachment to God; if ʿaṣr means time, misuse of time leaves people constantly losing.
rows.anchor: From a spiritual perspective, loss can also be seen as a reference to losing faith and attachment to God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Most call al-Māʿūn an early Makkan sūrah after al-Takāthur, though some assign vv. 4–7 to Madinah; since the whole sūrah addresses religious hypocrisy, it may all be Madinan, when hypocrisy could gain political advantage.
rows.anchor: commentators maintain that al-Māʿūn is an early Makkan sūrah

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Religious hypocrisy is not treated as limited to Muslims alone.
rows.anchor: Nonetheless, hypocrisy in religion was not seen as limited to Muslims alone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah takes its name from māʿūn in its last verse, broadly meaning kindness, charity, or assistance.
rows.anchor: The sūrah takes its name from the word māʿūn in the last verse, which in its widest sense indicates any act of kindness, charity, or assistance.

rows.speaker: IK
rows.claim: The verse describes people who perform devotions well but fail to act kindly toward others.
rows.anchor: This verse is understood to indicate those who perform their devotions well but do not act kindly toward others (IK).

rows.speaker: widespread interpretation
rows.claim: Māʿūn commonly means utensils or tools that neighbors share or lend, such as a pickax, pot, or bucket.
rows.anchor: a widespread interpretation that sees it as an allusion to utensils or tools that people would share and lend to one another

rows.speaker: others
rows.claim: Other interpretations take māʿūn as anything beneficial, obligatory zakāh, property generally in Qurayshi dialect, or refusing guests.
rows.anchor: It can also be seen as an allusion to anything in which there is benefit (Q). Many take refuse small kindnesses to indicate refusal to pay the obligatory zakāh

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All readings point to hypocrites' stinginess: they attend prayer lazily and spend reluctantly.
rows.anchor: According to all of these interpretations, the verse indicates the stinginess exhibited by hypocrites, who only come to the prayer lazily, and only spend reluctantly
